symbols.note: Main entry point for provider execution; handles rewrite and agentic modes, tracks writes, and falls back on errors.

claims.text: WHICH KIND of rewrite landed is provenance, not decoration: a windowed edit saw only a fragment of the file, so a reviewer reading 'rewrite' must not assume the model considered the whole document.
claims.why: The code distinguishes windowed vs full-file rewrites in the summary and handoff, and the comment accurately describes the provenance intent.

claims.text: if changed: how = ', '.join(f'{rel} ({"windowed" if rel in windowed else "full-file"})' for rel in changed); summary = f'Applied rewrite to: {how}.' else: summary = 'Rewrite produced no applicable change.'
claims.why: The code exactly implements this conditional logic.

claims.text: if skipped: summary += ' Skipped: ' + '; '.join(f'{k} ({v})' for k, v in skipped.items())
claims.why: The code appends skipped information to the summary as described.

claims.text: handoff: dict[str, Any] = {}; if windowed: handoff['windowed_rewrite'] = windowed; if skipped: handoff['skipped'] = skipped; if dropped: handoff['slice_context_dropped'] = dropped
claims.why: The code builds the handoff dict conditionally with those keys.

claims.text: return { 'status': 'done' if changed else 'needs_review', 'summary': summary[:600], 'files_changed': changed, 'tests_run': [], 'risks': [], 'todos': [], 'handoff': handoff }
claims.why: The return statement matches this structure exactly.

claims.text: BEFORE any prompt is built: every path below this line puts repository content on the wire (the rewrite prompt carries whole file bodies, the tool loop returns read_file results, the fallback inlines with allow_sensitive=True). None of that may reach an endpoint that is not this machine.
claims.why: The comment describes a security invariant about network egress. The code calls _refuse_if_remote() and native_chat(host=self.host) but does not show the full implementation of those functions or the network layer; the claim cannot be fully verified from this chunk alone.

claims.text: refusal = self._refuse_if_remote(); if refusal is not None: return {**refusal, 'persona': persona_for(self.caps.name, agent.get('name')), 'wrote': [], 'did_work': False}
claims.why: The code implements this exact refusal check and return.

claims.text: GROUND TRUTH for THIS call. Reset here (not only in __init__) so an instance reused across more than one run() never reports a PRIOR call's writes as this one's. _dispatch's write_file branch and _run_rewrite's write loop both append to self._written the moment a real target.write_text() succeeds -- never from the model's own self-reported files_changed. Being on self (not a local var) means it also survives an exception raised mid-_run_agentic, so the exception-fallback branch below still reports honestly instead of losing track of writes that already landed on disk before the model call that follows them failed.
claims.why: The comment describes behavior of _dispatch and _run_rewrite write loops that are not in this chunk. The reset of self._written = [] is visible (line 1172), but the claim about how writes are appended and surviving exceptions relies on code outside this chunk.

claims.text: NOTE: this key does NOT go inside `report` -- schemas.REPORT_KEYS is a closed set (validate_report rejects unknown keys, and that validation runs again downstream in verifier.verify), so 'wrote'/'did_work' live only on this outer dict, as siblings of 'report'.
claims.why: The claim references schemas.REPORT_KEYS and verifier.verify which are not in this chunk. The code does place 'wrote' and 'did_work' outside the report dict (lines 1185-1186, 1198-1199), but the constraints about REPORT_KEYS and validate_report cannot be checked here.
The line is present exactly as claimed.

claims.text: if writable and paths and len(paths) <= MAX_REWRITE_FILES: report = self._run_rewrite(...) else: report = self._run_agentic(...)
claims.why: The conditional branching matches the description.

claims.text: except (ProviderHTTPError, ValueError) as exc: Fall back to a single-shot advisory read if the tool loop can't run.
claims.why: The except block catches those exceptions and runs the fallback code.

claims.text: context, _ = read_inlined_context(paths, repo_root, MAX_CONTEXT_CHARS, allow_sensitive=True, policy=policy); system, user = build_prompt(agent, objective, context); msg = native_chat(...); report = coerce_report(extract_json(msg.get('content') or '{}'))
claims.why: The fallback code exactly follows this sequence.

claims.text: except (ProviderHTTPError, ValueError): wrote = list(dict.fromkeys(self._written)); return {'provider': ... 'wrote': wrote, 'did_work': bool(wrote)}
claims.why: The nested exception handler returns the error report with wrote and did_work as described.

claims.text: wrote = list(dict.fromkeys(self._written)); return {'provider': ..., 'persona': ..., 'agent': ..., 'report': report, 'wrote': wrote, 'did_work': bool(wrote)}
claims.why: The final return matches this structure.

observations.what: The run() method delegates to _run_rewrite or _run_agentic based on writability and path count, with a fallback to a single-shot advisory read on error.
Write tracking via self._written is reset at the start of run() and used to report actual writes even after exceptions.
The return from _run_rewrite includes a handoff dict with windowed_rewrite, skipped, and slice_context_dropped keys, and status 'done' or 'needs_review'.
The run() method returns wrote and did_work as top-level keys, separate from the report dict, to avoid schema validation issues.
